scenarios.title: Who is on my team?
scenarios.objective: Find a teammate before choosing whom to involve.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have the puck in a sharing activity. Navy2 wears navy like you; Gold1 wears gold. The coach asks you to find your teammate. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.

questions.prompt: Who is your teammate?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is on the same navy team as YOU. The labels also identify the teams.

questions.prompt: Which two things can you find here?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is your teammate and YOU have the puck. No goal has happened.

questions.prompt: Put this sharing routine in order.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested routine. Matching jerseys alone does not make a pass safe.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little nearer Navy2 without standing on Navy2.
questions.explanation: This example shortens the distance while keeping separate space. Other clear starting spots could work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 steps between you and Navy2. What could you do?

options.text: Shoot the puck away without looking for Navy2

questions.explanation: A teammate can become covered. Look again or find clearer space. Sending the puck away before you look can give Gold1 a chance to get it.

questions.prompt: Tell a grown-up how you found your teammate.
questions.explanation: Mention navy, the Navy2 label or the team introduction. Pointing is fine.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 takes the puck from YOU. What should you notice first?

options.text: Can I pass the old way?

questions.explanation: Gold1 now has the puck, so YOU must notice the change before deciding what to do. YOU cannot keep passing as though the puck were still yours.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 moves to a new spot while YOU hold the puck. Which two players should YOU keep track of?

options.text: Gold1, who may block the way
Only where Navy2 used to stand

questions.explanation: Check where Navy2 is now and where Gold1 is before choosing a pass. A teammate’s old spot may no longer be useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU with the puck to try a different passing angle toward Navy2.
questions.explanation: Try a controlled move that leaves a clear path toward Navy2 while keeping Gold1 in view. The puck stays with YOU. This is one example to discuss, not the only place that can work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 skates closer to YOU. Tell an adult what changed.
questions.explanation: A useful answer names Gold1 as closer pressure and Navy2 as a teammate to find. The next puck touch should follow that new picture.

scenarios.title: Room to carry
scenarios.objective: Notice an occupied route and a roomier practice area.
scenarios.briefing: YOU hold the puck. Gold1 is directly ahead. Navy2 waits off to one side. The coach invites you to explore the empty side away from Navy2. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 is ahead of YOUR facing direction.
Navy2 occupies one side of the practice area.
The opposite side has no player.

questions.prompt: Who is directly ahead of YOU?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is ahead in the direction YOU face.

questions.prompt: What is shown on the side away from Navy2?
questions.explanation: No player is placed on that side of the activity. Empty space does not guarantee an escape.

questions.prompt: Arrange this try at finding room.

options.text: Carry a short way and look again

questions.explanation: The routine invites another look when the situation changes.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into the empty practice space away from Navy2.
questions.explanation: This leaves the crowded line and the side Navy2 occupies. Other clear places may fit; a real route still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 moves into that empty space. What could you do?
questions.explanation: Notice the new player position instead of remembering one fixed spot.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you checked before carrying.
questions.explanation: Gold1, Navy2 or the empty ice are relevant observations. Speaking or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 covers your first angle, what should Navy2 see?

options.text: A different clear target or lane

questions.explanation: Gold1 removed the first window. A new angle or lane gives Navy2 a real choice if it is visible.

questions.prompt: After moving, what two players should YOU check?

options.text: Navy2, who is waiting for a pass

questions.explanation: YOU have the puck, so YOU choose the next play. Navy2 is the teammate who could receive it, and Gold1 could change the way there. Only the players in this picture can be checked.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in a spot where the way to Navy2 stays open.
questions.explanation: This spot keeps the way to Navy2 open and is closer to your partner than the empty-side example. Gold1 is still ahead in the middle, so check the way again after any move. Other open spots can work; the test is whether the path to Navy2 stays clear.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU pass to Navy2 and Navy2 now has the puck. How can you show you are ready for a return pass?
questions.explanation: This is a stated change: in the picture YOU still have the puck. After a pass, moving where Navy2 can see you and keeping your stick ready are ways to show it. Whether a return pass fits still depends on where Gold1 is.

scenarios.title: Listen for the practice stop
scenarios.objective: Recognize a stated practice stop signal.
scenarios.briefing: In this practice only, one whistle means stop under control and listen. It has just sounded. YOU hold the puck; Navy2 uses a separate lane. This is not a match restart rule. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: A practice stop signal was stated.

questions.prompt: What does this practice whistle mean?
questions.explanation: The briefing defines the signal for this activity.

questions.prompt: Which things help after that signal?
questions.explanation: Listening and awareness fit the instruction. These are suggested behaviours.

questions.prompt: Order this practice stop.
questions.explanation: The picture cannot measure stopping distance or technique.

questions.prompt: Is stopping the same as skating faster?

options.text: Yes, they both use your edges
Only when you are going fast

questions.explanation: Stopping and speeding up both use your edges, but they are different actions with different jobs. This practice signal asks for stopping under control.

questions.prompt: Now the coach invites a restart in your lane. What could you do?

options.text: Check the lane and begin gently
Start before the coach finishes talking
Assume every whistle has the same meaning

questions.explanation: Follow the new instruction. Waiting until the coach finishes and checking your own lane keeps the restart safe for both players. Another activity may use different signals.

questions.prompt: Tell a grown-up what you would listen for next.
questions.explanation: The next instruction or permission to begin is relevant. An adult can record spoken words.

questions.prompt: You have stopped, but the puck slides away. What could YOU do while the coach is talking?

options.text: Listen and ask before going to get it
Ask Navy2 to race after it

questions.explanation: Stay with the stop-and-listen instruction. Ask for help collecting the puck rather than starting another chase.

questions.prompt: Before turning to listen, what helps YOU give Navy2 room?

options.text: Keep your stick in your own space

questions.explanation: Notice your partner while you turn and leave room for both players and their sticks.

questions.prompt: The coach asks Navy2 to use more space for the next try. Move Navy2 farther from YOUR lane.
questions.explanation: This separates the two practice lanes. It is a new coach-directed setup, not permission to restart before the next signal.

questions.prompt: You did not hear what the coach said next. What could you say?
questions.explanation: Try “Can you say that again?” or “Can you show me?” Asking helps you know when and where to start the next try.

scenarios.title: A teammate behind your shoulder
scenarios.objective: Look beyond the forward direction to find a teammate.
scenarios.briefing: YOU face the attacking end and hold the puck. Navy2 is behind your facing direction. Gold1 is ahead on the other side. The coach asks you to find Navy2 before deciding on a puck action. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Navy2 is behind that facing direction.
Finding Navy2 does not prove a pass is open.

questions.prompt: Where is Navy2 compared with the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: YOU face the attacking end while Navy2 is behind YOU.

questions.prompt: What can looking around help you find?
questions.explanation: Teammate locations and pressure are the source-supported information cues.

questions.prompt: Arrange this looking activity.

options.text: Tell the coach where Navy2 is

questions.explanation: This is the activity routine. A screen answer does not demonstrate a real shoulder check.

questions.prompt: For a second try, move YOU away from the side with Navy2.
questions.explanation: This changes the viewing relationship while leaving space. It is a practice reset, not an ideal game position.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 skates ahead of YOU. Should you keep pointing behind?
questions.explanation: Locate the teammate again when their position changes.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you might miss by only watching the puck.
questions.explanation: Navy2 is a concrete example. A spoken answer or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves into the way ahead. What could YOU look for behind your shoulder?

options.text: Navy2 and a clear way to pass

questions.explanation: Navy2 is behind YOU. Looking there can reveal a different choice, but you still need a clear passing lane.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check before a pass back to Navy2?

options.text: Whether Gold1 can reach the passing lane
Only which way YOUR skates point

questions.explanation: A teammate behind you can help if you locate the target and check the lane. Facing forward does not remove the option of a pass back.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to a new waiting place behind YOU, with room for a short pass.
questions.explanation: Navy2 stays behind the way YOU face and separate from YOUR spot. Several nearby places can give a different passing angle.

questions.prompt: Why might a short pass back to Navy2 help you go forward later?
questions.explanation: It can move the puck away from Gold1’s pressure and give your team another view of the space ahead. Passing back is useful when that lane is clear; you do not have to use it every time.

scenarios.title: A mistake and another try
scenarios.objective: Respond kindly to a teammate error while noticing possession.
scenarios.briefing: In a friendly keep-away activity, Navy2 missed a pass and Gold1 gained the puck. The picture starts after that change. Navy2 looks to YOU for encouragement; the coach invites everyone to keep trying. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Everyone is invited to try again.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck after the missed pass?
questions.explanation: The current owner and stated event both identify Gold1.

questions.prompt: Which words could encourage Navy2?
questions.explanation: These are supportive examples. Other kind words may work too.

questions.prompt: Arrange one helpful response.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested routine, not the only acceptable order for showing support.

questions.prompt: For the next reset, find separate practice space near Navy2.
questions.explanation: This keeps YOU involved without occupying another player. It is a reset, not a defensive answer key.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU miss the next pass. What could help?
questions.explanation: A mistake can lead to another supported attempt.

questions.prompt: Say one kind thing you would like a teammate to tell you.
questions.explanation: Any respectful encouraging answer is welcome. An adult can record the child's own words.

questions.prompt: Gold1 has the puck now. What is a good first thing for YOU to do?

options.text: Notice who has the puck and where Navy2 is
Wait for the coach to tell YOU what happened
Skate to where the pass was going

questions.explanation: The puck changed hands, so the old plan is finished. Noticing the new owner and where your teammate is gives YOU something useful to do next.

questions.prompt: Which two things are true in this picture?

options.text: The pass to Navy2 did not finish
YOU are the navy player closest to the puck

questions.explanation: The picture starts after the miss, with Gold1 holding the puck. Navy2 is actually the navy player nearer the puck, so the third choice does not match what YOU can see.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in open space where Navy2 can find YOU for the next try.
questions.explanation: This gives YOU room on the far side from Gold1 and a short open route to Navy2 for the next try. It is one example spot; another open place can work. The picture does not prove Navy2 has already looked at YOU.

questions.prompt: What does “another try” mean after a missed pass?
questions.explanation: It means noticing what is true now, that Gold1 has the puck and Navy2 does not, and then getting ready to help again. Repeating the old pass plan without looking ignores where Gold1 is. Any answer in your own words is fine.
